246.title: Nachiketa and the worn-out cows
246.hook: a boy watches his father give away worn-out cows, and asks one question too many
246.tomorrow: three nights at Death's door, and nobody brings him water
246.howItsDone: Hindus tell the Katha's story of Nachiketa to children and also study it closely; Vedanta teachers, Shankara among them, wrote commentaries on it. In puja, families offer the deity fresh, whole fruit and flowers, not leftovers.

segments.voice: Last week, tadvana, the dear one: the gods' victory was never theirs. It was Brahman's, the divine mother reveals what the gods couldn't.

A charity drive at a big house. The owner is making a show of generosity, and his servants lead the gifts out one by one. But the kid in the doorway notices something. The gifts are the old stuff: cows that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and will never calf again. Everyone else nods politely. The boy can't. So begins the Katha Upanishad: a boy named Nachiketa, a father's careless gift, and, before long, Death.
screen: `A SHOW OF GENEROSITY.` → `THE OLD COWS.` → `THE BOY IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: The father, Vajashravasa, is performing a sacrifice where you're meant to give away everything you own. But his cows are worn out. The text says it bluntly: they've drunk their water, eaten their grass, been milked dry, and will bear no more. Joyless worlds, it says, await the one who gives gifts like these. Then: shraddha entered the boy. Shraddha is faith, trust, a deep seriousness; you met it in the Gita. It enters Nachiketa, still a child, and he goes to his father. Father, to whom will you give me? If the sacrifice means giving everything, the son belongs on the list. It's a real question, and a sharp one. The father doesn't answer. Nachiketa asks a second time, then a third. And the father, angry, the way a parent can be when a child sees through them in front of others, snaps: I give you to Death. To Yama. It's an ancient story, and a very modern one. A parent says something in anger they can't take back, and a child takes them at their word. Nachiketa doesn't run and hide. He thinks it through: I go first among many, in the middle of many. What will Yama do with me? He sees that people ripen and fall like grain, and rise again like grain. And he goes. Here's the first teaching of the week, and Hindus still live by it. An offering without shraddha is empty. The ritual was done, the cows were counted, and the text still calls those gifts joyless. That's why, in puja, families give God the fresh fruit and the whole flower, never the leftovers.
screen: `THE WORN-OUT COWS.` · `SHRADDHA ENTERED THE BOY.` · `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` · `I GIVE YOU TO DEATH.` · then, large: `NACHIKETA AND DEATH.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one small thing to offer today, a flower, a piece of fruit, a lamp, and pick the best one, not the leftover. Hold it for a breath, then offer it with your whole attention: that attention is the shraddha. If you don't pray, choose one real gift for someone this week, something that costs you a little, and give it whole.
Nachiketa. A boy whose father, angry, said: I give you to Death. Shraddha, faith, had entered him, and he went to Yama's house without fear.
Your line: offer the best, with shraddha. The boy saw what everyone else nodded past. Until tomorrow.

247.title: Three nights at Death's door
247.hook: three nights waiting at Death's door, and three wishes
247.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is as God
247.tomorrow: one wish left, and Death would rather not answer it
247.howItsDone: Hindu tradition treats the honoring of guests as sacred (atithi devo bhava, 'the guest is as God'); the Katha's opening is often told to show even Death keeping that duty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachiketa: old cows, a boy's question, to whom will you give me? And his father's angry answer: to Death.

A guest arrives, and nobody's home. He waits on the step. One night. Two. Three. Nobody brings him so much as a glass of water. The Katha takes that seriously: in a house where a brahmin guest waits without food, it says, the household's hopes, its good deeds, its children and its cattle are all put at risk. And this house belongs to Death. Nachiketa is sitting on its step, three nights in, still hungry.
screen: `WAITING ON THE STEP.` → `THREE NIGHTS.` → `THE HOUSE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Yama has been away. When he returns, his household tells him: a guest has been waiting, a young brahmin, like fire entering a house. Bring water. Yama is appalled. This is a teaching Hindus still live by, atithi devo bhava, the guest is as God, and even Death keeps it. He bows to the boy: you stayed three nights in my house without eating. For each night, choose a boon, a wish. Three wishes. Now watch what Nachiketa asks for. The first wish: let my father be calm again, no longer angry with me, and let him know me and welcome me when I'm sent back. Of all the things to ask of Death, he asks first that the relationship with his father be healed. Yama grants it: your father will sleep peacefully, and his anger will be gone. The second wish: teach me the fire ritual that leads to heaven, where there's no fear, no hunger, no old age. Yama teaches it, and is so pleased with how quickly the boy learns that he names the fire after him: the Nachiketa fire. He even adds an extra gift, a chain or garland. Two wishes, each one reasonable and generous, the kind a good son and a serious student would ask. The third waits for tomorrow. But notice who Nachiketa is so far: a boy who waits, who forgives first, who learns fast. The two paths are about to open in front of him.

segments.voice: Think of who might come through your door this week: family, a friend, a delivery driver, someone you didn't invite. If you pray, ask that your home be a place where a guest is met the way God is met, the way Yama bowed to a hungry boy. If you don't, simply choose one small welcome to offer: water first, a seat, a plate. And if someone is cross with you, borrow Nachiketa's first wish and wish them peace.
Vara, a boon, a chosen gift. Three nights at Death's door, then two boons: peace with his father, and the fire ritual that leads to heaven.
Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is as God. Even Death bowed to a hungry boy. Two hundred forty-seven days now.

248.title: The good and the pleasant
248.hook: the third wish, the best bribe ever offered, and a boy who turns it down
248.carry: shreyas, the good, over preyas, the pleasant
248.tomorrow: Death finally answers: what happens when we die?
248.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the Katha's shreyas and preyas, the good and the pleasant, as everyday language for moral choices; the passage opens the second section of the Katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vara: a boon for each of three nights at Death's door. Peace with his father, and the fire that leads to heaven.

There's a question people rarely say out loud. It comes at funerals, at three in the morning, in the hospital parking lot. When someone dies, what happens? Are they still, somewhere? Nachiketa is sitting across from the one being who would actually know. He has one wish left, and he asks it. What follows turns on a choice that shows up in small ways all day long: the good, or the pleasant.
screen: `THE THREE A.M. QUESTION.` → `ONE WISH LEFT.` → `HE ASKS IT.`

segments.voice: The third wish: when a person dies, there's this doubt. Some say they still are; some say they are not. Teach me this. Yama flinches. Even the gods doubted about this, he says. It's subtle, not easy to know. Choose another wish. Don't press me. Nachiketa doesn't budge: if even the gods doubted, and you say it's hard to know, then there's no teacher like you and no wish like this one. So Death tries a bribe. Sons and grandsons who'll live a hundred years. Herds of cattle, elephants, gold, horses. Land as wide as you like, and as many years as you want. Beautiful companions with chariots and music, rare among mortals. Enjoy them all. Just don't ask me about death. The boy says: these last only till tomorrow, Death. They wear out the sharpness of the senses. Even a whole life is short. Keep your horses, your songs and dances. No one is made content by wealth. Now Yama's tone changes. Many pleasures, he says, did not tempt you. And he teaches the two paths. One is shreyas, the good. The other is preyas, the pleasant. Both come to a person, and both bind. The wise one looks them over, tells them apart, and chooses the good over the pleasant. The foolish one chooses the pleasant, for the sake of getting and keeping. The pleasant isn't evil; it's what feels nice now. The good is what's actually good for you, and it often doesn't feel like much at first. Nachiketa just chose it, in front of Death.
screen: `WHEN SOMEONE DIES, WHAT THEN?` · `CHOOSE ANOTHER WISH.` · `KEEP YOUR HORSES AND SONGS.` · `THE GOOD, AND THE PLEASANT.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Picture one choice waiting for you today, the phone or the walk, the easy reply or the honest one, and set the two paths side by side. Feel how the pleasant pulls, and how quiet the good is. Hindu teachers call the power to tell them apart viveka, discernment; if you pray, ask for it. Then just look, the way the wise one in the Katha does, until the difference is plain.
Shreyas, the good, the better. Paired with preyas, the pleasant: both come to a person, and both bind. The wise look them over and choose the good; Nachiketa turned down the world for his question.
Your line: shreyas, the good, over preyas, the pleasant. Both paths come to everyone. That's day two hundred forty-eight.

249.title: The self is never born
249.hook: Death's answer: the self is not born and does not die
249.carry: the self is not born and does not die
249.tomorrow: who's really steering? Death draws a chariot
249.howItsDone: Bhagavad Gita 2.20, which closely echoes Katha 1.2.18, is often recited at Hindu funerals and memorials as the teaching that the self, the atman, is not born and does not die.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shreyas: the good and the pleasant both come to a person, and the wise choose the good.

If you read the Gita with us, today may bring a jolt of recognition. There's a verse you've heard before, in chapter two, when Krishna first tells Arjuna that the self can't be killed. Here it is again, almost word for word. Except now it isn't Krishna speaking on a battlefield. It's Death, speaking to a child. Most scholars think the Gita drew on the Katha. Today Yama finally answers the question.
screen: `A VERSE YOU'VE HEARD BEFORE.` → `NOT KRISHNA. DEATH.` → `THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Yama says: the knowing self is not born, and does not die. It didn't come from anywhere, and it didn't become anyone. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient: it is not killed when the body is killed. Then: if the killer thinks he kills, and the killed thinks he's killed, neither of them understands. This one does not kill, and is not killed. Those two verses reappear in the Gita, two nineteen and two twenty, with small changes. So Death's answer to what happens when we die: the self you really are, the atman, was never born, so it can't die. The body ends; the self doesn't. This is one of the deepest teachings in Hinduism, and it's why Hindu funerals speak of a body let go, not a person ended. Then Yama adds how this is known. The self is smaller than the small and greater than the great, hidden in the heart of every creature. It can't be gotten by lectures, or by brains, or by much learning. It's gained by the one it chooses; to that one it reveals its own nature. Commentators read that line differently. Shankara hears the seeker choosing the self alone. Theistic teachers like Ramanuja hear grace: the Lord chooses whom to reveal himself to. Both schools agree on the next line: not the one who hasn't turned from wrong, not the restless, not the scattered, can reach it by cleverness. That's why the two paths matter. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't a rule for its own sake. It's what makes the mind quiet enough to notice what was never born.
screen: `NOT BORN, AND DOES NOT DIE.` · `IT DOES NOT KILL; IT IS NOT KILLED.` · `NOT GAINED BY LEARNING.` · `THE ONE IT CHOOSES.` · then, large: `SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.`

segments.voice: Notice what in you has changed over the years: your body, your opinions, your face in photos. Then notice what hasn't, the plain sense of being here, aware, there at seven and here now, and rest in it for a few breaths. If someone you love has died, you can hold them in mind too; this is the teaching many Hindu families lean on at a memorial.

250.title: The chariot of the self
250.carry: the senses are horses; wisdom holds the reins
250.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of the Upanishads use the Katha's chariot to explain self, mind and senses, and some pair it with the Gita's picture of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aja: the self is not born and does not die, and it isn't gained by cleverness.

Driving home, and arriving with no memory of the drive. Something got the car there, but who, exactly? Or the opposite: the plan was to go straight home, and somehow the car is in the drive-through line. Who was steering? Yama knows the two paths are easy to name and hard to walk. So he gives Nachiketa a picture to carry, with a place in it for every part of a person: the body, the mind, the senses, and someone riding along. A chariot.
screen: `HOME, WITH NO MEMORY OF THE DRIVE.` → `WHO WAS STEERING?` → `A CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: Know the self as the rider in the chariot, Yama says, and the body as the chariot. Know the buddhi, the intellect, the part of you that discerns and decides, as the charioteer. The manas, the everyday mind, is the reins. The senses are the horses, and the things they chase are the roads. Picture them: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, each one strong, each pulling toward whatever it wants. The reins connect them to the charioteer, and the rider is the one the whole trip is for. Then Yama says what goes wrong. If the charioteer has no understanding, and the reins are always slack, the senses run wild like bad horses. That's the drive-through line. If the charioteer understands and holds the reins steady, the senses are like good horses: all their strength, going where they should. Notice he doesn't say kill the horses. Horses are the power; you need them. The point is who holds the reins. And where does the road go? The one whose charioteer is wise, whose reins are steady, reaches the end of the road, which the text calls the highest place of Vishnu, the all-pervading. It's one of Hinduism's clearest maps of a person: atman, body, buddhi, manas, senses. And it's the two paths in one picture. The pleasant path lets the horses choose the road. The good path has the charioteer choose it, and the horses run there gladly. Some readers hear an echo of it in the Gita, where Krishna is Arjuna's actual charioteer.
screen: `THE RIDER, AND THE CHARIOT.` · `CHARIOTEER, REINS, HORSES.` · `WILD HORSES, OR GOOD HORSES.` · `THE END OF THE ROAD.` · then, large: `THE CHARIOT OF THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Feel your senses as horses, and notice which one is pulling hardest right now: a sound, an itch, hunger, the phone. Don't fight it; feel the reins in your hands and draw them in gently, not yanking, just steadying, until each horse settles. Then sit as the charioteer, reins held lightly, the rider behind you at rest.
Ratha, chariot. Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.

251.title: Arise, awake
251.hook: arise, awake; the path is sharp as a razor's edge
251.carry: arise, awake: turn the gaze within
251.tomorrow: how the Katha ends, and whether Death keeps the boy
251.howItsDone: Katha 1.3.14, 'uttishthata jagrata', was taken up by Swami Vivekananda as a call to awaken, and Hindu teachers quote it as a call to wake up to the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ratha: the chariot of the self. Rider, charioteer, reins and horses.

Ever been woken by someone who really needed you up? Not a gentle alarm. A hand on the shoulder, a voice: get up, now. One verse in the Katha sounds exactly like that: short, urgent, impossible to sleep through. Swami Vivekananda took it up as a rallying cry for his listeners. It's possible to know the line well without knowing it came from the house of Death.
screen: `A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.` → `GET UP, NOW.` → `FROM THE HOUSE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Right after the chariot, Yama says: uttishthata, jagrata. Arise! Awake! Having reached the great teachers, learn. Then a warning: the path is sharp as the edge of a razor, hard to cross, hard to walk, say the wise. Step carelessly and you're cut. That doesn't make it cruel. It makes it narrow. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't done once; it's done step by step, with attention. A few verses later, Yama explains why the path is hard. The self-existent one, he says, pierced the openings of the senses outward. So eyes, ears and attention point away, by design, not at the self within. But some wise person, wishing for the deathless, turned their eyes inward and saw the self. The phrase is often translated as turning the gaze around. And what's seen? A person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body, like a flame without smoke. Lord of past and future. The same today and tomorrow. That's the teaching: the self lives within, in the heart, and you find it by turning inward, with a teacher's help. Having reached the great ones, learn: that's the guru, and why Hindus seek one. Three ways of saying it. Arise, awake: the sleeper drifts toward the pleasant. The razor's edge: the good path is narrow and needs care. The inward gaze: the senses face out, and the good path turns them back. None of it is gloomy. A flame without smoke is waiting when you stop looking only outward.
screen: `ARISE! AWAKE!` · `SHARP AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `THE SENSES FACE OUTWARD.` · `A FLAME WITHOUT SMOKE.` · then, large: `TURN THE GAZE AROUND.`

segments.voice: Open your eyes and notice how naturally they go outward, to the room, the light, whatever moves. Now close them and turn the gaze around: not looking at anything, just feeling the place you look from. If it helps, picture a small, steady flame in the center of the chest, smokeless and warm; if not, simply rest behind your closed eyes.
Uttishthata, arise. The good path is sharp as a razor's edge, and it turns the gaze inward. Awake, and learn.
Your line: arise, awake: turn the gaze within. The good path is narrow, not cruel. See you tomorrow.

252.title: The knots of the heart
252.hook: a tree with its roots in the sky, the knots of the heart, and a boy set free from death
252.carry: moksha: the heart's knots cut, even here
252.tomorrow: one syllable, om, and everything in it
252.howItsDone: Students of Vedanta read the Katha with commentaries such as Shankara's; its closing chapter defines yoga as the steady holding of the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, uttishthata: arise, awake. The path is sharp as a razor's edge, and the wise turn the gaze around to find a flame without smoke.

A boy was given to Death by an angry father. He waited three nights hungry at Death's door, turned down every pleasure in the world, and asked the question Death itself didn't want to answer. A story like that could end with a bargain lost, or a little time won before Death comes back. Not this one. In the Katha's last pages, Death finishes teaching. And the boy walks out of Death's house free.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `NOT A BARGAIN LOST.` → `THE BOY WALKS OUT FREE.`

segments.voice: Near the end, Yama gives three last pictures. First, a tree: the eternal ashvattha, a sacred fig, with its roots above and its branches below. The world hangs down from what's above it, like a tree upside down. The Gita opens chapter fifteen with the same tree. Second, yoga. When the five senses are still, with the mind, and the intellect doesn't stir, that's called the highest state. Yama defines yoga as that firm holding of the senses. Not a pose. A steadiness: the reins from the chariot, held firm. Third, the heart. When all the desires that dwell in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal, and reaches Brahman here. When all the knots of the heart are cut, even in this life, the mortal becomes immortal. Hindus call that freedom moksha. Not escape from the world; a heart with its knots untied, even in this life. Then the last verse. Nachiketa, having received this knowledge from Death, and the whole method of yoga, reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death. And so will anyone, the text says, who knows the self this way. That's the week. Old cows and a boy's shraddha. Three nights at Death's door. The good and the pleasant. The self not born, not dying. The chariot. Arise, awake. And the knots of the heart, cut.
screen: `THE TREE WITH ROOTS ABOVE.` · `YOGA: THE SENSES HELD STILL.` · `THE KNOTS OF THE HEART, CUT.` · `NACHIKETA, FREE OF DEATH.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to the center of your chest and notice if there's a knot there right now: a worry, a want, a grudge. Don't try to cut it; breathe toward it, the way you'd breathe on cold hands, and let the senses go still one at a time, eyes resting, ears resting, the body quiet. That steadiness, the Katha says, is yoga; if the knot loosens even a little, notice that.
Ashvattha, the sacred fig with roots above and branches below. Nachiketa chose the good, learned from Death, and walked out free. That's the Katha.
Your line: moksha, the heart's knots cut, even here. Tomorrow, twelve verses and one syllable: om. That's day two hundred fifty-two.
